title: O-1 'Extraordinary Ability' Visa Gains Traction as H-1B Gets Tougher and Costlier
excerpt: With the H-1B lottery oversubscribed and new fees looming, Indian tech professionals are pivoting to a merit-based visa with no cap — and no luck required.
body:
• The O-1 visa — for individuals with "extraordinary ability" — has no annual cap, no lottery, and no wage-weighted selection, making it an increasingly attractive alternative to the H-1B.
  • Immigration attorneys report an unprecedented surge in O-1 inquiries in 2026 as H-1B costs rise and selection becomes more competitive under the new wage-based system.
  • A Bengaluru software engineer's story of landing an O-1 after three H-1B rejections has gone viral, inspiring thousands of Indian tech professionals to explore the option.
  • USCIS has responded with a surge in Requests for Evidence (RFEs), demanding more rigorous documentation from O-1 applicants.

The H-1B Problem

The H-1B visa has long been the default path for skilled Indian professionals entering the U.S. workforce. In 2026, that path has become considerably harder to walk.

The implementation of a wage-weighted selection process means employers offering higher salaries get priority in the lottery, pushing out entry-level and mid-career applicants who once competed on equal footing. Proposed new fees for certain petitions filed from abroad have made the process more expensive. And with FY 2027 cap registrations already exhausted, the numbers speak plainly: the H-1B is more competitive and cost-prohibitive than it has ever been.

Enter the O-1.

What the O-1 Actually Requires

The O-1 visa is designed for individuals who have demonstrated "extraordinary ability" — defined by USCIS as "a level of expertise indicating that the person is one of the small percentage who have arisen to the very top of the field of endeavor."

That sounds intimidating. In practice, immigration lawyers say the bar is reachable for many mid-career professionals who have never thought of themselves in those terms. The O-1A category covers sciences, education, business, and athletics. The O-1B covers arts, film, and television.

Applicants must meet at least three of eight criteria, which include nationally or internationally recognized awards, published research, membership in professional associations that require outstanding achievement, evidence of original contributions of major significance to the field, and authorship of scholarly articles.

"Instead of waiting on luck, I went all in on what I could control: late nights, building products, publishing research, and contributing to the field I love. Turns out, consistency pays better than the lottery."

— Tanush Sharanarthi, software engineer who secured an O-1 after three H-1B rejections

Why It Matters Now

The advantages over the H-1B are structural. The O-1 has no annual cap and no lottery — approval is based on merit, not random selection. There is no maximum period of stay, compared with the H-1B's six-year limit. It can be filed at any time during the year, and there is no degree requirement. Perhaps most importantly, O-1 holders are well-positioned for the EB-1A green card category, which does not require employer sponsorship — a significant advantage for professionals trapped in decade-long green card backlogs.

The Law Office of Andrew R. Sones, which provides immigration services nationwide, reports seeing "an unprecedented increase in O-1 inquiries" in 2026. Other immigration firms confirm the trend, noting that the combination of H-1B uncertainty, rising fees, and the proposed $100,000 OPT work permit charge has made alternatives more urgent.

The USCIS Response

The surge has not gone unnoticed. USCIS has responded with a significant increase in Requests for Evidence — formal demands for additional documentation before a case can be approved. Immigration attorneys warn that the era of streamlined O-1 approvals may be ending, and that applicants must now present meticulously documented petitions with extensive supporting evidence.

The key, lawyers say, is preparation. Applicants should begin building their O-1 portfolio well before they need to file — assembling evidence of publications, patents, awards, media coverage, and peer recognition over months or even years. A rushed petition with thin documentation is increasingly likely to trigger an RFE or an outright denial.

The Diaspora Calculation

For Indian tech professionals — who account for the largest share of H-1B petitions annually — the O-1 represents a fundamentally different immigration strategy. Rather than relying on employer sponsorship and lottery luck, it rewards sustained professional achievement and positions applicants for faster green card processing through the EB-1A category.

The trade-off is effort. Building an O-1 case requires deliberate career investment: publishing research, speaking at conferences, contributing to open-source projects, earning peer recognition. But for professionals already doing that work, the visa may be hiding in plain sight.
